newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's generals in political arena to stay.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's generals in political arena to stay.

text.p: Cheered on by a fractious elite united only by its distaste for the ruling Islamists, the armed forces have once against staked their claim to a place in Turkey's democracy.

Despite a lull, force commanders are quietly pressing ahead with a campaign against what they see as the creeping Islamisation of public life -- in direct challenge to the elected government of Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan.

In recent weeks they have ordered the civilian leadership to cut back severely on Koranic education, demanded new restrictions on pro-Islamist media and taken the lead in foreign policy, in particular targeting the Islamic Republic of Iran.
But the generals need not use brute force to get the government to comply. The army has considerable influence over the media and the rightist wing of Erbakan's shaky coalition.

The army's decisive style and high standing have been seen by much of the public as a welcome antidote to the secularist parties, whose squabbling opened the door to Erbakan and his Welfare Party despite its slim plurality of just 21 percent.
As a result, say analysts and commentators, it will now be next to impossible to get the soldiers out of the political arena and back to barracks any time soon.
"Democracy had three legs, namely, the legislative, executive and judicial," said Mehmet Ali Birand, a commentator and an authority on the Turkish military's role in politics.
"Now we have created a fourth with our own hands. From now on we will live with a military democracy. From now on the military will be part of the system," Birand wrote in the daily Sabah.

The generals, never far from the surface of Turkish politics since handing power back to the civilians in 1983, have nonetheless been re-invigorated by challenging Erbakan to clamp down on the very Islamist activists who make up his core voters.

Elements of the mainstream media and a number of political figures have egged on the army to depose Erbakan's uneasy coalition with pro-Western conservatives led by Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller. For now, such coup talk remains just that -- talk.

But an earlier show of strength, in which army tanks paraded through an Islamist district, won widespread approval. More recently, the secularist majority has taken to booing Islamists at public gatherings, including football matches and concerts.

Through the National Security Council, a constitutional body they dominate, the commanders on February 28 issued a declaration to Erbakan, modern Turkey's first Islamist leader, spelling out 18 measures against religious activism.

Press leaks suggest the generals used a second meeting, on March 31, to keep up the pressure on Erbakan without openly repeating earlier demands. They have also continued to speak out through selected newspaper columnists.
This quiet pressure has left few in Turkey in doubt that the armed forces, who have brought down three governments in the last four decades, are still playing to win.
Already, there is talk of a late April deadline for compliance with their demands. However, no time limit has been made public.
"The tensions were not dispelled by the second meeting of the Security Council. In fact, the military and the government have burned their bridges," analyst Bilal Cetin told Reuters.
"No government in the history of the Turkish Republic has been so isolated," said Cetin. "If you likened Turkey to a company, then the army holds 51 percent of the shares."
But what of the end game? Can the army, which has bet its considerable prestige on crushing the Islamists, follow through without unleashing its ultimate weapon -- the coup d'etat?

"Both sides know the stakes but no one can control the process," said a senior European envoy. "They will fence, trying to postpone the inevitable clash," he said, adding the conflict would likely build slowly through the summer.
This go-slow approach by the military, widely venerated as the country's most efficient and powerful institution, reflects the clear recognition that times have changed.
Any move to send in the tanks would prove messy -- at least politically.
Gone are the days when the armed forces' patrons in Washington, eyes firmly on the Soviet threat, were prepared to overlook anti-democratic moves in the name of Cold War security.
Diplomats from the European Union, which Turkey hopes one day to join, have also made it clear where they stand.
"This would set Turkey back 20 years," said the senior EU diplomat. "And we have told the Turks that."
